title: Qantas - Project Sunrise
body:
O.P.
Is this the last frontier for non-stop air travel to anywhere in the world? Creating this thread to discuss ideas re aircrafts, configurations, would people be welcoming it with open hands and what would it mean for those one stop flights currently connecting these cities. I (personally) feel there are implications for lots of other airlines if Qantas (and Boeing or Airbus) can pull this through and make it a reasonable experience at the same time.
SIA now flying the SIN-EWR route, Qantas will be watching the experience and the performance of this route to further refine their ideas and requirements. Would they make it a premium only service like SIA or keep it all inclusive like their current PER-LHR service.
Like this simple slide on Qantas website.
https://www.qantasnewsroom.c om.au/wp-content/uploads/201 7/08/Project-Sunrise-Fact-Sheet.pdf

[User #742437061 postsTheDocWhirlpool Forums Addict] individualist writes...
Is this the last frontier for non-stop air travel to anywhere in the world?
No. Not even close.
Distance is only one of the factors that results in the requirement for stopovers – popularity of the route is the other main one.
For example, the US mainland is 3,000 miles wide – there have been aircraft that can cover that distance for countless years, yet most flights still involve 2 (or sometimes 3) legs. Why? Because there isn't the demand for a direct flight from Palm Springs, California to Chattanooga, TN.
Similarly, even if it's possible for Qantas to fly from Sydney to Paris and London, there won't be the demand for them to also fly to Amsterdam and Frankfurt and Munich and Budapest, and so on...
Airlines like Emirates, Turkish, Wow, and many others, with their single-hub model and well-timed bank flights will continue to make up the majority of travel, even if we do see more and more non-stop flights covering the ultra-popular routes.
Australia is a little unique in the sense that more than half the population lives within the catchment area of 3 airports (SYD/MEL/BNE) which makes it a little easier to have direct flights to "all" major airports for at least one end of the flight, but there's no other continent where this is true.

I recently flew LHR to PER on QF10 and then connected in Perth on a direct flight to Canberra. Compared to LHR-SIN-SYD-CBR the total travel time was 5-6 hours less.
With good winds the flight time was a little over 16 hours, versus the 14 hours from SYD to DXB on the way to Europe. Although personally I think once you get over 9 or 10 hours there's not much difference between 14 and 17 hours.
My seats this time were purchased with points but if I was flying again and the price was relatively close I would choose the direct LHR-PER option every time.
